morose

muh-ROHS · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Morose is gloomy, bad-tempered, and withdrawn -- sad in a way that shuts other people out.

Ever since the team lost the finals, the star player has been morose, barely speaking to his teammates at practice.

Example

The usually chatty barista had gone morose all week, answering every question with a one-word grunt and avoiding eye contact with customers.

Morose combines sadness with a sullen, withdrawn irritability -- it's not just quiet sadness, but sadness mixed with a bad mood.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

broody: Broody means sunk in silent, gloomy thought -- a person brooding turns a worry over and over inside. Morose adds a prickly, bad-tempered edge to that gloom: the broody friend is lost in thought, while the morose one snaps when you interrupt.

sulky: Sulky is silent bad temper over a specific grievance -- a child denied dessert sulks and gets over it. Morose is heavier weather: a settled gloom, withdrawn and irritable, that hangs on without needing any one slight to explain it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

cheerful: noticeably happy or optimistic

genial: friendly and warm in manner

Where it sits · how deeply the bad mood settles in — glum → morose → embittered

glum vs. morose: Being glum for an afternoon after bad news is normal and passes quickly -- far shallower than morose, which settles in and sours a person's whole manner for days.

embittered vs. morose: Someone embittered has let long-term resentment sour their whole outlook, beyond a temporary morose mood.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — mor-

root — mor-: manner, custom, habit (Latin mos, moris)

suffix — -ose

suffix — -ose: full of, given to (Latin -osus)

Put it together

Put it together: Morose comes from Latin morosus ("peevish, particular about one's habits"), from mos/mor- ("custom, manner") -- someone fussy about their own ways, which drifted to mean sullen and bad-tempered.

Use the root in a new word: mores

Use the root in a new word: mores: Every culture has its own mores, the customs and manners its people are expected to follow.
